title: As if seen
hook: live among people as if God saw you, speak to God as if people heard
carry: the private and public self become one

segments.voice: Yesterday: Stilpo, in fallen Megara, and your line, you won't lose yourself. Did you keep your short list of what can't be taken? Day four hundred forty-four.

Behind a closed door, where nobody will ever know, small choices get made: whether to return the extra change, whether to read the message over someone's shoulder, whether to say the unkind thing in a private chat. The person making them isn't always the one the world sees. Seneca's tenth letter is about being alone, and it ends with a sentence that closes the gap between the two versions of us from both directions. Today: Athenodorus.
screen: `WHEN THE DOOR IS CLOSED.` → `TWO SLIGHTLY DIFFERENT PEOPLE.` → `AS IF SEEN.`

segments.voice: First, a warning about being alone. Seneca tells a story about Crates, the Cynic. He saw a young man walking by himself and asked what he was doing out there alone. I'm talking with myself, the young man said. Crates answered: be careful, then, you're talking with a bad man. Solitude is only good, Seneca says, if the company inside is good. Second, the open prayer. Then Seneca passes on a saying of Athenodorus, a philosopher he quotes. You'll know you're free of your cravings, he said, when you ask God for nothing that you couldn't ask for openly, in front of everyone. Seneca notes how many people whisper prayers they'd be ashamed for others to hear. Third, the sentence. And then Seneca's own line: live among people as if God were watching; speak with God as if people were listening. Two directions. When you're with others, act as you would before the highest witness you know. When you're alone with the highest, ask only for what you'd be glad to have heard. Fourth, the witness. Seneca says God here. Listeners of any faith may hear that word in their own way, and those without one can think of the best witness they can imagine. The point is the same either way. A life lived as if seen, by someone kind and clear-eyed, doesn't need two versions. The person behind the closed door and the person in the crowd can finally be the same.
screen: `CRATES: TALKING WITH A BAD MAN.` · `ASK ONLY WHAT YOU'D ASK OPENLY.` · `LIVE AS IF GOD SAW YOU.` · `ONE PERSON, NOT TWO VERSIONS.` · then, large: `AS IF SEEN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you've been wishing for privately, a hope you haven't said out loud. Now imagine saying it plainly in a room full of people who know you. Would you be glad for them to hear it? Don't judge the answer. Just notice whether the wish changes shape when it's said in the open. If you pray, this is Athenodorus' test: could you ask it in front of everyone? If you don't, it works on any wish. The bell holds the time.
Athenodorus. The philosopher Seneca quotes: you'll know you're free of your cravings when you ask God for nothing you couldn't ask for openly, in front of everyone.
Your line: the private and public self become one. Once today, when no one is watching, act as if someone kind and clear-eyed were. Day four hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Some people, religious and not, try to act in private as they would before a kind and clear-eyed witness, so that their private and public lives match.

original.note: Latin: as if God sees, from Seneca's tenth letter.

trapdoor: what you thought: behave because someone's watching.
what it means: Seneca says live among people as if God saw you, and speak with God as if people heard, so there's one self, not two.
what a scholar hears: the Latin is two matched halves, sic vive cum hominibus tamquam deus videat, sic loquere cum deo tamquam homines audiant: one about public conduct, one about private prayer.

notes: Review (2026-10-01): hook no longer opens 'Think about' or says 'most of us'; Athenodorus no longer labeled a Stoic (Seneca does not say so here); cut the Stoic-God doctrine gloss and 'many faiths'; practice now uses Athenodorus' open-asking test so it doesn't duplicate day 445's watcher practice.

Letter 10.1: Crates and the young man walking alone ('cave, inquit, et diligenter attende: cum homine malo loqueris'); 10.5: Athenodorus' saying on asking God only for what you can ask openly; 'sic vive cum hominibus tamquam deus videat; sic loquere cum deo tamquam homines audiant'. Paraphrased; confirm.
Athenodorus: probably Athenodorus Cananites, teacher of Augustus; confirm identification.
The practice offers 'if you pray, this might be God' as an option, not a requirement; no new prayer is written.
Classical Latin pronunciation used for 'tamquam deus videat'.
